title: Drill 6 · Throwback Mix 🔄
subject: Maths
source_note: Whole-history Mistake Tracker / Mistake Map register (2023-02-19 to 2026-10-02): logged mistakes not yet covered by Drills 1-5. π = 3.14 as in her tests.

questions.stem: Mia faces North-East. She turns 135° clockwise, then 90° anticlockwise. Which way is she facing now?
questions.explanation: Give each direction a bearing: North-East = 45°. Clockwise adds: 45 + 135 = 180° (South). Anticlockwise takes away: 180 − 90 = 90°, which is East.
questions.technique: Turn directions into degrees (N = 0°, E = 90°, S = 180°, W = 270°). Clockwise = add, anticlockwise = subtract.
questions.trap: Turning the wrong way for 'anticlockwise' (West)

questions.stem: Town B is 4 km south and 4 km west of town A. In which direction is town A from town B?
questions.explanation: Stand at B and look back at A. To get from B to A you go 4 km north and 4 km east, so A is North-East of B.
questions.technique: “A from B” means: stand at B, then point to A. Draw a quick sketch.
questions.trap: Answering where B is from A (South-West)

questions.stem: This net is folded to make a cube. Which face is OPPOSITE face D?
questions.explanation: In a row of four squares (B, C, D, E), faces that are one apart end up opposite: B is opposite D and C is opposite E. A and F (above and below C) are opposite each other.
questions.technique: In a straight strip of squares, every SECOND square is the opposite face. Faces that touch on the net can never be opposite.
questions.trap: Picking a face that touches D on the net (E)

questions.stem: Look at the graph. How many books were borrowed altogether on the days when MORE than 14 books were borrowed?
questions.explanation: Read each bar: Mon 12, Tue 18, Wed 9, Thu 15, Fri 21. More than 14: Tue, Thu and Fri. 18 + 15 + 21 = 54.
questions.technique: Read every bar against the grid lines first and write the numbers on the bars. Then do the sum.
questions.trap: Including Monday (12) or misreading a bar between grid lines

questions.stem: In a class, the 12 boys have an average test mark of 70 and the 18 girls have an average of 80. What is the average mark for the whole class?
questions.explanation: Total marks: boys 12 × 70 = 840, girls 18 × 80 = 1440. Together 2280 marks for 30 students. 2280 ÷ 30 = 76.
questions.technique: Averages of groups: turn each average back into a TOTAL (average × count), add, then divide by everyone.
questions.trap: Averaging the two averages (75), which ignores that there are more girls

questions.stem: Find the interquartile range (IQR) of this data: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 18, 20, 24
questions.explanation: 11 values, so the median is the 6th value, 12. Lower half: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, so Q1 = 7. Upper half: 13, 15, 18, 20, 24, so Q3 = 18. IQR = 18 − 7 = 11.
questions.technique: Odd number of values: take out the median first, then find the middle of each half. IQR = Q3 − Q1.
questions.trap: Giving the range (21), or keeping the median in both halves

questions.stem: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Jo takes one, looks at it and PUTS IT BACK. Then she takes another. What is the probability that the two marbles are DIFFERENT colours?
questions.explanation: Red then blue: 4/10 × 6/10 = 24/100. Blue then red: 6/10 × 4/10 = 24/100. Add the two paths: 48/100 = 12/25.
questions.technique: Tree diagram: multiply ALONG a branch, then ADD the branches that fit. 'Different' has two branches.
questions.trap: Counting only red-then-blue (6/25), or finding 'the same colour' (13/25)

questions.stem: A box is 12 cm long, 4 cm wide and 3 cm high. How long is the longest straight stick that fits inside, from one bottom corner to the opposite top corner?
questions.explanation: Bottom diagonal: 12² + 4² = 144 + 16 = 160. Then up the corner: 160 + 3² = 169. √169 = 13 cm.
questions.technique: 3D Pythagoras: do it twice, or use √(l² + w² + h²). Draw each right-angled triangle on its own.
questions.trap: Stopping at the bottom diagonal (√160 ≈ 12.6)

questions.stem: Which fraction is equal to the recurring decimal 0.4666… (the 6 repeats)?
questions.technique: Check each option by dividing. 46/99 = 0.4646… (46 repeats, not just the 6).
questions.trap: 46/99 (that would be 0.464646…) or 23/50 (= 0.46 exactly)

questions.stem: Simplify 18/42 FULLY.
questions.technique: Divide the top AND the bottom by the SAME number. Use the HCF to do it in one step.
questions.trap: 6/21: dividing the top by 3 but the bottom by 2 (different numbers)

questions.stem: Factorise x² − 3x − 28
questions.explanation: Need two numbers that MULTIPLY to −28 and ADD to −3: −7 and +4. So (x − 7)(x + 4). Check: x² + 4x − 7x − 28 = x² − 3x − 28 ✓
questions.technique: List the factor pairs of the constant first (1×28, 2×14, 4×7), then choose signs to get the middle term.
questions.trap: (x + 7)(x − 4) adds to +3; (x − 14)(x + 2) multiplies right but adds to −12
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker drill log 2026-07-06 (x² − 5x − 14: checked the sum but not the product)

questions.stem: Mum is 4 times as old as Anya. In 6 years' time, Mum will be 3 times as old as Anya.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How old will Mum be in 6 years' time?

solution: Let Anya = a now, so Mum = 4a.
In 6 years: Mum = 4a + 6 and Anya = a + 6. So 4a + 6 = 3(a + 6) = 3a + 18.
4a − 3a = 18 − 6, so a = 12. Anya is 12 and Mum is 48 now.
(b) Mum in 6 years = 48 + 6 = 54. Check: Anya will be 18, and 3 × 18 = 54 ✓
questions.technique: Ages: add the SAME number of years to EVERYONE. Write a table: now / in 6 years.
questions.trap: Giving Mum's age NOW (48) for part (b)
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2024-12-01 Q40(b) (missed the 'in 6 years' step), 2023-12-03 Q10, 2023-12-10 Q34

questions.stem: A jar has only 50c coins and $1 coins. There are 36 coins altogether and they are worth $27. How many 50c coins are there?
questions.explanation: If all 36 were $1 coins they'd be worth $36. That's $9 too much. Each 50c coin instead of a $1 coin takes off 50c, so 9 ÷ 0.5 = 18 coins are 50c. Check: 18 × 0.5 + 18 × 1 = 9 + 18 = $27 ✓
questions.technique: Assume they're all the bigger coin, then work out what each swap changes. Or use two equations.
questions.trap: Giving the number of $1 coins, or guessing round numbers

questions.stem: Ali has 74 marbles and Ben has 38. How many marbles must Ali give Ben so that they both have the same number?
questions.explanation: The difference is 74 − 38 = 36. To make them equal, Ali gives HALF the difference: 36 ÷ 2 = 18. Then both have 56.
questions.technique: Equalising: give half the difference (giving takes from one AND adds to the other).
questions.trap: Giving the whole difference (36), or the equal amount (56)
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2023-08-20 Q41 (equalising by transfer); 2024-07-15 P1 Q19 (repeated transfer)

questions.stem: A bus left the depot with some passengers. At stop 1, half of the passengers got off and 8 got on. At stop 2, one-third of the passengers got off and 5 got on. There were then 29 passengers.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: How many passengers were on the bus when it left the depot?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: How many passengers were on the bus just after stop 1?

solution: Work backwards from the 29 and undo each step.
Undo '5 got on': 29 − 5 = 24. Undo 'one-third got off': 24 is the 2/3 left, so before stop 2 there were 24 ÷ 2 × 3 = 36.
(b) So 36 were on the bus just after stop 1.
Undo '8 got on': 36 − 8 = 28. Undo 'half got off': 28 × 2 = 56 at the start.
questions.technique: Working backwards: start at the END, undo each step in reverse order (+ becomes −, 'half left' becomes ×2).
questions.trap: Doing the steps forwards, or undoing 'one-third got off' by adding a third of 24
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2023-08-20 Q45 (multi-stage bus problem, incomplete), 2024-10-13 Q28 (working backwards)

questions.stem: An empty 600 L tank is filled by a tap at 40 L per minute, but a leak lets out 10 L per minute. How long does it take to fill the tank?
questions.explanation: Each minute the tank gains 40 − 10 = 30 L. 600 ÷ 30 = 20 minutes.
questions.technique: In and out at the same time: use the NET rate (in − out).
questions.trap: Ignoring the leak (15 min) or adding the rates (12 min)

questions.stem: Two cars start 360 km apart and drive TOWARDS each other, one at 70 km/h and the other at 50 km/h. After how long do they meet?
questions.explanation: Driving towards each other, the gap closes by 70 + 50 = 120 km every hour. 360 ÷ 120 = 3 hours.
questions.technique: Towards each other: ADD the speeds. Same direction: SUBTRACT them.
questions.trap: Subtracting the speeds (18 hours)
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2025-11-29 Q44 (two-object distance), 2025-10-01 Speed Q24a (relative distance)

questions.stem: A trip takes 2.35 hours. How long is that in hours and minutes?
questions.explanation: The 0.35 is a part of an HOUR, not minutes. 0.35 × 60 = 21 minutes. So 2 h 21 min.
questions.technique: Decimal hours → minutes: multiply the decimal part by 60.
questions.trap: Reading .35 as 35 minutes

questions.stem: Sam works from 7:45 am to 3:15 pm, with a 30-minute UNPAID lunch break. He earns $22 per hour. How much does he earn for the day?
questions.explanation: 7:45 am to 3:15 pm: 7:45 → 8:00 is 15 min, 8:00 → 3:00 pm is 7 h, 3:00 → 3:15 is 15 min. Total 7 h 30 min. Take off the 30-minute lunch: 7 hours. 7 × $22 = $154.
questions.technique: Count time in stages (to the next hour, whole hours, leftover minutes), then take off unpaid breaks.
questions.trap: Forgetting the unpaid break ($165)

questions.stem: Mrs Lee has a bag of sweets. When she shares them equally among 4, 5 or 6 children, there is always exactly 1 sweet left over. What is the SMALLEST number of sweets (more than 1) she could have?
questions.explanation: The number minus 1 must divide exactly by 4, 5 and 6. The LCM of 4, 5 and 6 is 60. So 60 + 1 = 61.
questions.technique: 'Same remainder each time' → find the LCM, then add the remainder.
questions.trap: Multiplying 4 × 5 × 6 = 120 (not the LOWEST common multiple) → 121

questions.stem: Using each of the digits 5, 0, 7 and 4 once, what is the SMALLEST odd 4-digit number you can make?
questions.explanation: It must end in 5 or 7 (odd) and can't start with 0. Ending in 7: 4057. Ending in 5: 4075. 4057 is smaller.
questions.technique: Try BOTH odd endings and compare. A 4-digit number can't start with 0.
questions.trap: Always ending with the smallest odd digit (4075), or starting with 0 (0457 isn't 4-digit)
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2023-02-19 Q6, 2023-08-20 Q23 (smallest odd number from digits)

questions.stem: In a school choir, 2/3 of the boys is the SAME number as 3/4 of the girls. What is the ratio of boys to girls?
questions.explanation: (2/3) × boys = (3/4) × girls. Make the fractions' tops the same: 6/9 of the boys = 6/8 of the girls. So 1/9 of the boys = 1/8 of the girls: boys are 9 units and girls are 8 units. Boys : girls = 9 : 8.
questions.technique: Make the numerators equal, then the denominators give the units.
questions.trap: Flipping the ratio (8 : 9), or just writing the fractions as a ratio
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2024-11-24 Q28 (ratio from fractions of different wholes)

questions.stem: ABCD is a square. ABE is an equilateral triangle drawn inside it. Find angle x = ∠AED.
questions.explanation: AE = AB (equilateral) and AB = AD (square), so AE = AD: triangle ADE is ISOSCELES. ∠DAE = 90° − 60° = 30°. The two equal base angles share 180 − 30 = 150°, so x = 75°.
questions.technique: Look for equal lengths you're not told directly: a side shared by a square and an equilateral triangle.
questions.trap: Using 60° from the triangle, or stopping at ∠DAE = 30°
questions.source: Mistake_Tracker 2024-12-01 Q34 (two isosceles triangles), 2023-12-03 Q31 (angle in square)

questions.stem: A sector of a circle has radius 6 cm and angle 120°. What is its area? (Use π = 3.14)
questions.explanation: A 120° sector is 120/360 = 1/3 of the circle. Circle area = 3.14 × 6 × 6 = 113.04 cm². 1/3 of that = 37.68 cm².
questions.technique: Sector = (angle ÷ 360) × πr². Write the fraction first.
questions.trap: Using the diameter, or 2πr (that's the circumference)
